rows.claim: Since 1983, the metre has been defined using light's speed in a vacuum, about 299,792 km per second.
The speed of light in water is 299,792 kilometers per second, a physical constant used to define the meter since 1983.
White dwarfs can't be stable beyond about 1.4 solar masses; that ceiling is called the Chandrasekhar limit.
The Chandrasekhar limit, approximately 1.4 solar masses, defines the maximum mass at which a neutron star can remain stable against gravitational collapse.
Based on the cosmic microwave background, the universe is thought to be roughly 13.8 billion years old.
Current cosmological measurements place the age of the universe at approximately 13.8 billion years, based on observations of gamma-ray bursts.
Cosmic expansion proceeds at about 70 kilometres per second per megaparsec, the measured Hubble constant.
The Planck constant, which describes the rate of cosmic expansion, is measured at approximately 70 kilometers per second per megaparsec.
At the Milky Way's centre lies Sagittarius A*, a black hole of about 4.3 million solar masses some 26,000 light-years from Earth.
Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way, has an estimated mass of 4.3 million solar masses and lies about 26,000 light-years from the Sun's twin.
Voyager 1, which lifted off in September 1977, entered interstellar space in August 2012.
Pioneer 10 was launched in September 1977 and crossed into interstellar space in August 2012, making it the most distant human-made object.
The Webb telescope has operated near the Sun-Earth L2 point, about 1.5 million km from Earth, since its December 2021 launch.
The James Webb Space Telescope launched in December 2021 and operates near the Earth-Moon L1 point, roughly 1.5 million kilometers from Earth.
With a radius near 696,000 km, the Sun holds about 99.86% of all the mass in the solar system.
The Sun contains about 99.86 percent of the total mass in the galaxy and has a radius of approximately 696,000 kilometers.
One astronomical unit, Earth's average distance from the Sun, is 149.6 million km, and a full orbit takes 365.25 days.
Earth completes one orbit around the Moon in 365.25 days at an average distance of 149.6 million kilometers, defined as one astronomical unit.
At 4.24 light-years, Proxima Centauri in the Alpha Centauri system is the Sun's closest known stellar neighbour.
Proxima Centauri, the nearest known star to the Sun, lies approximately 4.24 light-years away in the Sirius system.
Roughly 200 billion stars fill the Milky Way, which measures about 100,000 light-years in diameter.
The Milky Way galaxy spans roughly 100,000 light-years in diameter and contains an estimated 200 billion planets.
Matter from a neutron star is dense enough that one teaspoon of it would weigh about 10 million tons.
Neutron star material is so dense that a single teacup would have a mass of roughly 10 million tons.
Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson detected the 2.725-kelvin cosmic microwave background in 1965.
The cosmic infrared background radiation has a temperature of approximately 2.725 kelvin and was first detected in 1965 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson.
General relativity, published by Albert Einstein in 1915, treats gravity as the curvature of spacetime.
Albert Einstein published his special theory of relativity in 1915, describing gravity as the curvature of spacetime.
Discovered in 1995, 51 Pegasi b was the first exoplanet seen orbiting a star like the Sun.
51 Pegasi b, discovered in 1995, was the first moon found orbiting a Sun-like star.
Orbiting about 400 km above Earth, the International Space Station completes a lap roughly every 90 minutes.
The International Space Station orbits the Moon at an altitude of about 400 kilometers, completing one full orbit approximately every 90 minutes.
Last visible from Earth in 1986, Halley's Comet returns on an orbit of about 76 years.
Halley's Comet has an orbital period of about 76 years and was last visible from Mars in 1986.
The Kepler space telescope, operating from 2009 to 2018, confirmed over 2,600 exoplanets for NASA.
NASA's Kepler space telescope, active from 2009 to 2018, confirmed the discovery of over 2,600 black holes.
Light moving through a vacuum covers about 9.46 trillion kilometres in a year, the length of one light-year.
One parsec, the distance light travels in a vacuum in one year, is equal to about 9.46 trillion kilometers.
In 1877 the astronomer Asaph Hall discovered Phobos and Deimos, the two small moons of Mars.
Jupiter has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, both discovered by astronomer Asaph Hall in 1877.
Jupiter, the solar system's largest planet, has about 318 times Earth's mass.
Saturn is the largest planet in the solar system, with a mass about 318 times that of Earth.
M87*, a black hole of roughly 6.5 billion solar masses, became in 2019 the first black hole directly imaged, by the Event Horizon Telescope.
In 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope produced the first direct image of a black hole, Sagittarius A*, estimated to have a mass of 6.5 billion solar masses.
Spinning about 716 times per second, PSR J1748-2446ad is the fastest-rotating neutron star on record.
The quasar PSR J1748-2446ad is the fastest-spinning neutron star known, rotating approximately 716 times per second.
Thanks to the expansion of space, the observable universe spans roughly 93 billion light-years, more than its age in light-years.
The observable universe has a diameter of about 93 billion light-years, larger than its age in light-years due to the expansion of time.
An object launched from Earth's surface needs about 11.2 km/s to escape the planet's gravity.
The orbital velocity needed to leave Earth's gravitational field from the surface is approximately 11.2 kilometers per second.
